lead: Qudos Eetho Sunday opens the West Syriac year. Before the Church speaks of the Annunciation and the Birth of the Lord, she looks at herself: a people God has made holy and chosen as his dwelling. The Old Testament lessons follow that dwelling through Israel's history: the Tabernacle in the desert (the lectionary prints Exodus 10:1–5; the setting up of the Tabernacle in Exodus 40 seems to be meant), Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 6:1–8), the glory of the Lord leaving the Temple in Ezekiel's vision (Ezekiel 10), and Isaiah's vision of the Holy One in the Temple (Isaiah 6:1–8). The Catholic Epistle (1 Peter 2:1–12) calls the baptised living stones of a spiritual house, and the Evening Gospel (Mark 8:27–30) gives Peter's confession in its shortest form.

This study takes three of the readings, which build on one another. Solomon builds a house for the Lord with stones prepared in silence. Paul says that Christ has broken down the wall between peoples and is building one holy temple with himself as the cornerstone. In Matthew, Jesus himself says, “on this rock I will build my church.” The key words are house, stone and building: God is the builder, Christ is the foundation, and we are the stones.

r.h: A house for the Lord, built in silence
set: 1 Kings tells how David's son Solomon came to the throne (chapters 1–2), asked God for wisdom (chapter 3) and organised his kingdom (chapters 4–5). Chapters 6–8 are the heart of his story: the building and the dedication of the Temple. David had wanted to build a house for the Lord, but through the prophet Nathan God answered that he would build a “house” for David, a lasting dynasty, and that David's son would build a house for God's name (2 Samuel 7:11–13). Solomon builds with cedar sent by Hiram, king of Tyre (1 Kings 5).

The Temple stood on the hill to the north of the city of David, which the Chronicler identifies with Mount Moriah (2 Chronicles 3:1). Its plan, a porch, a long main hall and an inner room, is like that of other temples of the region, but its meaning is new: there is no image of God inside, only the ark of the covenant under the wings of the cherubim (6:23–28; 8:6–9).
str: v. 1: the date, counted from the Exodus.
vv. 2–3: the size of the house and of its porch.
vv. 5–6: side rooms in three storeys built around the house.
v. 7: stone prepared at the quarry; no sound of iron at the holy place.
v. 8: the stairway to the upper storeys.

¶ The number 480 is probably a round, symbolic figure: twelve generations of forty years. It ties the Temple to the Exodus. The people set loose from Egypt now receive a house where God dwells among them. On the traditional reckoning, the work began in the middle of the tenth century BC.
kw: The same word means a building and a family line. In 2 Samuel 7 God plays on both meanings: David will not build God a house; God will build David a house. In Matthew 16 Jesus too speaks as the builder: “I will build my church.”

The hêkāl is the long main hall; the word goes back to an old word for a palace, a “great house”. The dᵉbîr is the innermost room, a perfect cube of twenty cubits (6:20), the Holy of Holies where the ark rested.

Literally “whole stone”. The related form is used for the altar of “unhewn stones” on which no iron tool was to be lifted (Deuteronomy 27:5–6). The word comes from the same root as šālôm, peace, and as the name Solomon (Šᵉlōmōh).
vv: In the four hundred eightieth year after the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build the house of the Lord.

The Temple is dated from the Exodus, not only from the king's reign. Israel's release from Egypt reaches its goal in worship: “Let my people go, so that they may worship me” (Exodus 8:1). Ziv, the month of “brightness” or blossoms, falls in spring (April–May).
The house that King Solomon built for the Lord was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high.

A cubit was about 45 cm, so the house was about 27 metres long, 9 metres wide and 13.5 metres high: smaller than many parish churches today. Its glory lay not in its size but in the One who chose to dwell there.
The house was built with stone finished at the quarry, so that neither hammer nor ax nor any tool of iron was heard in the temple while it was being built.
The noise and the cutting happened elsewhere; at the holy place the stones were only fitted together. The house of God rose in silence, assembled rather than forced.
ch: Solomon himself knew that no house could contain God: “Even heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you, much less this house that I have built!” (8:27). The Catechism recalls Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the Temple (CCC 2580), and teaches that Jesus spoke of his own body as the true Temple (John 2:19–21; CCC 586). The Church herself is called God's building and temple (CCC 756). St Bede, in his work On the Temple, reads the stones shaped at the quarry as believers prepared in this life by trials and grace, so that in the heavenly Jerusalem they may be set in place in peace, without the sound of hammers (in substance).

r.h: Christ the cornerstone of one holy temple
set: Ephesians is a letter written from prison (3:1; 4:1) to Christians who were mostly Gentiles by birth. Chapters 1–3 praise God's plan to gather all things in Christ; chapters 4–6 show how to live it. Just before our passage Paul reminds his readers that they were once “without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel”, but now “you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (2:12–13).

In the Temple rebuilt by Herod, a low stone barrier separated the outer court, open to Gentiles, from the inner courts. Notices in Greek warned foreigners not to pass it, on pain of death; two of these inscriptions have been found. Many commentators think Paul has this barrier in mind when he speaks of “the dividing wall”. Paul himself was arrested in Jerusalem on the charge of bringing a Gentile into the Temple (Acts 21:28–29).
str: vv. 14–16: Christ is our peace: the wall is broken down, one new humanity is created, and both are reconciled to God through the cross.
vv. 17–18: he proclaimed peace to the far and the near; through him both have access in one Spirit to the Father.
vv. 19–22: the image of the house: citizens, household, foundation, cornerstone, temple, dwelling.
¶ Verse 18 is quietly Trinitarian: through the Son, in the Spirit, to the Father. That is the shape of all Christian prayer, and of the anaphora at every Holy Qurbono.
kw: A rare word, found only here in the New Testament: a wall in the middle, a partition.
The right to be brought into the presence of a king. Through Christ, Jew and Gentile alike may approach the Father (compare 3:12; Romans 5:2).

The word comes from the Greek text of Isaiah 28:16, “a precious cornerstone”, which today's Catholic Epistle also quotes (1 Peter 2:6). It may mean the corner foundation stone that sets the line of the whole building, or the keystone at the top. Either way, everything holds together in Christ.
A permanent home, not a tent for a journey. God's purpose is to live among his people.
vv: For he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.
Paul does not only say that Christ brings peace, but that he is our peace. Peace is a person before it is an agreement.
for through him both of us have access in one Spirit to the Father.
So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God,
The outsiders become family. The Greek word for “members of the household” (oikeioi) comes from the same root as “house”.
built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone.
The prophets here are probably the prophets of the early Church, named with the apostles again in 3:5 and 4:11. The Church rests on their witness, and Christ holds the whole building together.
In him the whole structure is joined together and grows into a holy temple in the Lord;
A building that grows: Paul joins the language of architecture with the language of life, as 1 Peter does with “living stones”. The Church is never finished in this age; every baptism adds a stone.
ch: The Second Vatican Council gathers these images: the Church is “the building of God”, built on the foundation of the apostles, with Christ as the cornerstone, a holy temple which the Fathers saw pictured in churches built of stone (Lumen Gentium 6). The Catechism calls the Church the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is to the Body of Christ what the soul is to the body (CCC 797). Preaching on the anniversary of a church's dedication, St Augustine told his people that the building is the house of their prayers, but they themselves are the house of God, built when they come to faith and joined together by love (in substance; Sermon 336).

r.h: On this rock I will build my church
set: Caesarea Philippi lay at the foot of Mount Hermon, where one of the springs of the Jordan comes out of a cave in a great rock face. Herod's son Philip had rebuilt the town and named it in honour of the emperor, and the cave was a shrine of the Greek god Pan. Far from Jerusalem, among the shrines of other gods and of Caesar, Jesus asks who he is. The scene is a turning point: from here Matthew's Gospel turns toward Jerusalem and the cross (16:21).
Matthew follows Mark 8:27–33 (today's Evening Gospel is the first part of it), but adds the words of Jesus to Peter in vv. 17–19, which are found only in Matthew.
str: vv. 13–14: what people say: John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah, one of the prophets.
vv. 15–16: “But who do you say that I am?” Peter's confession.
vv. 17–19: Jesus' answer: a beatitude, a new name, a promise, the keys.
v. 21: the first prediction of the Passion.
vv. 22–23: Peter objects and is rebuked.

¶ The reading holds two sides of Peter together. In v. 18 he is the rock on which Christ builds; in v. 23 he becomes a stone to trip over. The same man is blessed when he receives the Father's revelation, and rebuked when he thinks as mortals do.
kw: In Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke, the one word Kêphâ serves for both, which is why Peter is also called Cephas (John 1:42; 1 Corinthians 1:12). Greek needed a masculine name, Petros, beside the common noun petra, but the play on words is plain: “You are Rock, and on this rock I will build.”

In the Greek Old Testament this word translates qāhāl, the assembly of Israel gathered by God, as at Sinai. In the Gospels it appears only here and in 18:17. Jesus speaks of “my church”: the people of God gathered anew around him.

An echo of Isaiah 22:22, where the steward of the royal palace receives “the key of the house of David”, to open and to shut. The keys stand for authority over the house, given as a steward's service.
Jewish teachers used these words for forbidding and permitting, and for imposing or lifting a ban. In 18:18 the same power is given to the disciples together.
A stone that trips the feet. The rock of v. 18 becomes a stone in the way when Peter tries to keep Jesus from the cross.
vv: Simon Peter answered, “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.”
Matthew's form is fuller than Mark's (“You are the Messiah”, Mark 8:29). Peter confesses not only a role, Messiah, but a relationship: Son of the living God.
Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah! For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven.
“Flesh and blood” is a Semitic way of saying “human beings”. Faith is a gift before it is an achievement (compare 11:25–27).
And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.
The verb is future, and Christ is the builder: “I will build”. The “gates of Hades” are the power of death. The Church may suffer, but death will not swallow her.
I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven,
“Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me; for you are setting your mind not on divine things but on human things.”

In Greek, “Get behind me” (hypage opisō mou) is close to Jesus' first call to Peter, “Follow me” (deute opisō mou, 4:19). Peter is not sent away; he is sent back to his place, behind the Master, as a disciple. “Satan” recalls the tempter in the desert, who also offered a way without the cross, and whom Jesus sent away with the same word (4:8–10).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Church is built “on the rock of this faith confessed by St Peter” (CCC 424), and also that Christ made Peter himself the rock of his Church and gave him the keys (CCC 552–553, 881). These are not rival readings. The Fathers spoke of the rock as Peter, as Peter's faith and as Christ himself; St Augustine, late in life, set two of these readings side by side and left the choice to his readers (in substance; Retractations I.21). The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Bishop of Rome, as successor of Peter, is the lasting and visible source and foundation of unity for the bishops and the faithful (Lumen Gentium 23; CCC 882).

qa: Is the rock Peter, or Peter's faith?

The Catholic answer holds both together. Jesus gives the name to the person, Simon, and the play on words points to him (CCC 552, 881). But Peter is the rock as the one who confesses the faith the Father revealed to him (CCC 424). Christ remains the one foundation and the cornerstone (1 Corinthians 3:11; Ephesians 2:20); Peter is the rock by sharing in his firmness, as a gift for the whole Church.

Not because Peter was possessed or rejected. “Satan” means adversary. Out of love, Peter was repeating the tempter's suggestion: a Messiah without the cross. Jesus sends him back behind him, to follow. The same Peter later followed his Lord to a cross of his own (John 21:18–19).
Does Ephesians 2:15 mean that God rejected the Law of Moses?

No. Paul speaks of the law “with its commandments and ordinances” in its role as a wall that kept Jews and Gentiles apart, such as the rules of food and purity. In Christ that separating role ends, and both become one people. The moral law is fulfilled, not cancelled (Matthew 5:17), and the Church honours the Jewish people, whose gifts and calling from God are irrevocable (Romans 11:29; Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839).
rite: The Malankara year does not begin with Advent, as in the Latin Church, but with two Sundays of the Church: Qudos Eetho, the Sanctification of the Church, and Hoodos Eetho, the Dedication of the Church. Only then does the season of the Annunciations (Suboro) lead us toward the Birth of the Lord. The order itself teaches: everything we celebrate in the year, we celebrate as the Church that God has made holy.

Today's Gospel has a special meaning for us. The Church of Antioch, mother of the West Syriac tradition, honours St Peter as its first bishop. In 1930 Archbishop Mar Ivanios and his companions, keeping the ancient Antiochene liturgy, entered full communion with the Bishop of Rome, the successor of Peter. A Malankara church consecrated with holy Myron is a sign of what we are: living stones, built on the faith of Peter, with Christ as the cornerstone. And when we sing “Holy, holy, holy” at the Holy Qurbono with the seraphim of Isaiah 6, the small parish church joins the worship of heaven.
study: Solomon's stones were shaped at the quarry and fitted in silence. Where is God shaping me now, so that I may fit into his house?
Ephesians 2:14 says that Christ is our peace. Is there a “dividing wall” in my family, parish or village that I am keeping up?
Jesus asks, “But who do you say that I am?” How would I answer in my own words today?
Peter was a rock and a stumbling block in the same chapter. When have I tried to keep Jesus, or someone else, away from the cross?
